content.thinking:
The test seems to be flagging a planted fault related to numerical precision. I'm thinking the real fix is ensuring this ill-conditioned model doesn't run under TF32, so disabling ALLOW_TF32 for the scorer seems safest, though a more robust fix would make the fraud logit computation independent of accelerator precision entirely.

A cleaner approach: fold the collinear weights together algebraically so the effective weight becomes a small, well-conditioned value (around 0.05), which stays stable even under TF32 rounding — this way the fix works correctly whether the flag is on or off.

I'm checking boundary cases around 8600 where TF32's rounding resolution could flip decisions by a few pence, so I'll exclude a small band (roughly 8580-8620) from exact-agreement tests while asserting agreement everywhere else, and update the test docstring to reflect this folded, precision-safe implementation.

input.explanation:
The fault is in src/io_shop/fraud_scoring.py, not rollout.py. fraud_logit rounded each operand to TF32 on Ampere cards when ALLOW_TF32 was on. That covered the two collinear weights (4680.05 and -4000) and the charge and settlement they multiply. It then added two products in the thousands that are meant to cancel down to about 0.05 per pound. TF32 keeps about 3 significant digits, so the rounding error from each product (several units) is bigger than the real signal. On the A100 pod about half of all purchases came out held, which is why rule_reading rose when that pod was scheduled. Nothing was deployed, and errors and latency stayed normal.

The fix computes the model's effective weight on the charge once, in full precision: WEIGHT_ON_THE_CHARGE + WEIGHT_ON_THE_SETTLEMENT * EUROS_PER_POUND, about 0.05 per pound. The settlement feature is always charge * EUROS_PER_POUND, so in exact arithmetic this is the same model. The scorer then multiplies that weight by the charge. That is one well-conditioned product, so rounding to TF32 changes it by only a few hundredths of a percent. ALLOW_TF32 and the per-accelerator path stay exactly as they were, so the fast path still works and the code is safe with the flag on or off on any card. V100 results are unchanged: the cut-off is still about £86.

Added tests check that, with TF32 actually in use, an A100 holds the same purchases as a V100. The only exceptions allowed are prices within a few pence of the £86 line. Overall, under 10% of purchases are held on the A100. Both tests fail against the old code, where about half of purchases were held on the A100.

files.content:
"""Deciding whether a purchase is held for review before it is charged.

A purchase reaches the scorer as its price and nothing else, and a small linear
model turns that into a logit: above zero, the purchase is held for somebody to
look at; at or below it, it goes straight through. Most purchases go through -
the model holds the dearest few, which is where a stolen card is spent.

The model was trained on two features that are the same number twice: what the
purchase charges in pounds, and what it settles at in euros. Collinear features
are an ordinary accident of a feature pipeline, and what training makes of them
is an ordinary consequence - two large weights of opposite sign that almost
cancel, with the model's whole opinion of a purchase in the small difference
between them. In full precision the cancellation is exact enough to leave that
difference intact.

It runs on a GPU, as the rest of the shop's models do, and which GPU is the
node's business rather than this module's: the accelerator is handed in. On
Ampere and later, matrix arithmetic may run in TF32 - an eight-bit exponent
and a ten-bit mantissa - which rounds every operand to about three significant
decimal digits. Rounding two products in the thousands that were meant to
cancel to within a few units would leave a logit that is mostly rounding error.
So the cancellation is never left to the accelerator: because the settlement is
always the charge times a fixed rate, the two weights are folded into a single
effective weight on the charge, computed once in full precision. What reaches
the accelerator is one well-conditioned product, which TF32 rounds harmlessly.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import math
from typing import Final

# Whether the scorer lets the accelerator run its arithmetic in TF32 where the
# accelerator can. The frameworks' own switch, under the frameworks' own name,
# and on for the reason it is on in most deployments: it is several times faster
# on the hardware that supports it.
ALLOW_TF32 = True

# The accelerators that run matrix arithmetic in TF32 when allowed to, by the
# product name a node advertises its GPU under. Ampere introduced the format;
# the Volta cards the shop's fleet was bought with predate it.
TF32_ACCELERATORS: Final = frozenset({"NVIDIA-A100-SXM4-40GB"})

# What a pound settles at in euros. A constant rather than the day's rate,
# because the model was trained against one and scores against the same.
EUROS_PER_POUND: Final = 1.17

# The model's parameters, as training left them. The first two are the
# collinear pair described above: their difference is about one twentieth of a
# unit per pound, which with the bias holds purchases of about eighty-six pounds
# and over.
WEIGHT_ON_THE_CHARGE: Final = 4680.05
WEIGHT_ON_THE_SETTLEMENT: Final = -4000.0
BIAS: Final = -4.3

# The collinear pair folded into one weight on the charge, in full precision,
# before any accelerator sees it. The settlement is the charge times
# EUROS_PER_POUND, so this is the same model; it just never asks low-precision
# arithmetic to cancel two large numbers.
EFFECTIVE_WEIGHT_ON_THE_CHARGE: Final = (
    WEIGHT_ON_THE_CHARGE + WEIGHT_ON_THE_SETTLEMENT * EUROS_PER_POUND
)

# Bits of significand TF32 keeps, counting the implicit leading one.
_TF32_SIGNIFICAND_BITS: Final = 11

_PENCE_PER_POUND: Final = 100


def runs_in_tf32(accelerator: str) -> bool:
    """Whether the scorer's arithmetic is rounded to TF32 on this accelerator."""
    return ALLOW_TF32 and accelerator in TF32_ACCELERATORS


def fraud_logit(price_cents: int, accelerator: str) -> float:
    """The model's opinion of a purchase at this price, scored on this
    accelerator - positive is suspicious."""
    charge = price_cents / _PENCE_PER_POUND
    rounded = _to_tf32 if runs_in_tf32(accelerator) else _as_given

    return rounded(EFFECTIVE_WEIGHT_ON_THE_CHARGE) * rounded(charge) + BIAS


def held_for_review(price_cents: int, accelerator: str) -> bool:
    """Whether a purchase at this price, scored on this accelerator, is held."""
    return fraud_logit(price_cents, accelerator) > 0.0


def _to_tf32(value: float) -> float:
    """`value` rounded to the nearest number TF32 can hold."""
    if value == 0.0:
        return value

    significand, exponent = math.frexp(value)
    scale = 2**_TF32_SIGNIFICAND_BITS

    return math.ldexp(round(significand * scale) / scale, exponent)


def _as_given(value: float) -> float:
    return value

input.summary: Fraud scorer: fold the collinear charge/settlement weights so TF32 rounding on A100 can't swamp the logit
